title: Assembling the Mind's Mosaic: EEG Semantic Intent Decoding
one_liner: Read a person's intended meaning from brain signals by breaking meaning into small, reusable semantic pieces and reassembling them into sentences.
lead: A brain-computer interface translates thoughts into words. Today's BCIs either force users to pick from a fixed list of words or generate gibberish because they treat meaning as a shapeless blob. This paper breaks meaning into named semantic units (the ideas that make up a sentence) and shows how to rebuild sentences from them, making BCIs both more expressive and interpretable.

problem.h2: Brain-to-text is stuck between two bad choices
paras: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) — systems that read signals from the brain and convert them to computer commands — are the frontier of accessibility. Today the problem is that no current method handles natural, open-ended thoughts well. Either you lock users into choosing from a small fixed vocabulary (like picking from a menu of 100 allowed words), which is clunky and unnatural; or you let the system generate any word it wants, which produces nonsense because the neural signals are noisy and the system loses track of what it was saying mid-sentence.

Both approaches fail at the core problem: they never say what meaning actually is. A person thinking the word apple does not activate a single special brain pattern labeled apple. Instead their brain lights up with a cluster of related ideas — the shape, the taste, the fact that it is red, the time you ate one, the sound of the word. Those ideas overlap with thoughts about oranges and tomatoes. If a BCI system does not understand that meaning is built from reusable pieces, it cannot translate thoughts into natural language.

callout.html: Decode meaning by identifying which reusable semantic pieces (objects, actions, qualities) light up in brain signals, then assemble them into grammatical sentences.

steps.text: Sensors measure electrical activity across the scalp as the person thinks.
A neural network finds which idea-chunks (objects, actions, qualities) activated in the brain.
Assign each activated chunk to the semantic unit it corresponds to, like matching puzzle pieces.
Use grammar rules to decide which pieces go first and how to connect them.
Spell out the intended meaning in a complete, grammatical sentence.

paras: The paper changes how BCIs represent meaning during decoding. Instead of treating each word as an isolated label, it treats meaning as a set of named semantic units — discrete idea-chunks like 'agent', 'action', 'object', 'quality', 'location'. This shift from labels to units is the core move.

hidden.name: how much each semantic unit contributes
paras: The hidden quantity is the activation level of each semantic unit — how strongly each named idea-chunk fires in the brain during a specific thought. When a person thinks about a red apple, the units for color, shape, food, and object all activate to different degrees. The paper measures this by having a neural network read EEG signals and output a score for each unit. High score means the unit is present in the thought; low score means it is absent.

The paper estimates this by using a technique called set matching — imagine laying out all possible semantic units like cards on a table, then marking which ones the EEG pattern 'lights up'. This is more flexible than old methods that forced a yes-or-no decision for each word independently.

heat.caption: Darker means the semantic unit is more active in the decoded thought.

reads.html: When you think of an action, certain regions of your brain light up with the idea of 'doing something' — this is the semantic unit for action. The paper measures which units activate by looking at the EEG pattern.
Set matching assigns each activated EEG cluster to its closest semantic unit from a predefined vocabulary, producing a sparse set of active units per thought.

mechanism.h2: Why semantic units fix the communication problem
paras: The problem with old BCIs is that meaning is not a single thing; it is a bundle of related concepts. When the old system tried to classify 'is this apple or orange', it threw away all the other relevant information — the fact that both are round, both are food, both are colors. By forcing a binary choice, it lost the structure of meaning. BrainMosaic does not force that choice. Instead it identifies all the semantic units that are present in the thought at once — the person can activate object, color, action, and texture simultaneously. This is closer to how the brain actually works.

Here is the mechanical chain: (1) EEG signals encode a distributed pattern of brain activity tied to the person's intended thought; (2) a neural network maps that pattern to a set of semantic units by asking 'which concept-chunks explain this EEG signal'; (3) because multiple units can be active at once, the system captures the full compositional structure of the meaning (red + object + falling); (4) a reconstruction module then generates a sentence that uses all those units, ensuring coherence. The advantage over fixed-class classification is that new combinations of units produce new meanings without retraining — the space of expressible thoughts expands combinatorially.

stages.s: Set matching identifies active semantic units

math.words: The paper uses a matching score between the decoded semantic units and a reference vocabulary. For each thought, it computes the best-fitting subset of semantic units by maximizing the alignment (how many units are correctly matched) while minimizing false positives.
math.equation: semantic_units = argmax_U sum_i match(U_i, EEG_signal) - lambda * |U|
symbols: the set of active semantic units in the thought
how well unit U_i explains the observed EEG
a penalty weight; controls sparsity (fewer units vs. accuracy)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose for the thought 'red apple': EEG matches 'object' with score 0.92, 'color' with 0.88, 'food' with 0.79, 'texture' with 0.45, 'emotion' with 0.12.
With lambda = 0.15 (slight penalty per unit): sum of matches (top 3) = 0.92 + 0.88 + 0.79 = 2.59; penalty for 3 units = 0.15 * 3 = 0.45; net score = 2.59 - 0.45 = 2.14.
If we add 'texture' (score 0.45): new sum = 3.04, penalty = 0.60, net = 2.44 (worse). So the model selects only the top three units: object, color, food.

math.note: The equation picks the semantic units that best explain the EEG, while avoiding noise and spurious units.

charts.title: Old fixed-class BCI
charts.note: Fixed vocabulary means high accuracy for memorized words but fails when combining units into new phrases.

charts.title: This paper (semantic units)
charts.note: Semantic units compose into new meanings because the system can recombine units in ways never seen during training.

items.html: If a person activates a semantic unit that the model was never trained to recognize (e.g., a very specific cultural reference), the system will not decode it. The vocabulary must be broad enough to cover the user's experience.
Some brain states activate multiple overlapping semantic units equally. The set matching algorithm may pick the wrong subset, producing a grammatically correct but semantically wrong sentence.
The reconstruction module uses fixed grammar rules. If a user's thought does not fit standard word order (e.g., poetic or emphatic structure), the system will flatten it into conventional form.

When users are well-trained (they learn to activate units consistently) and the semantic vocabulary matches their lived experience, the system produces fluent, natural sentences that capture nuanced meanings.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo would record EEG from a person thinking five different thoughts (e.g., 'red apple', 'falling slowly', 'on the table', 'beautiful morning', 'sad memory'). For each thought, the BrainMosaic system should output the semantic units it detected and the corresponding sentence. To compare: run a fixed-class BCI on the same recordings and show that it either fails to express the thought or produces a generic label. Measure both fluency (is the sentence grammatical?) and semantic accuracy (does it match the intended thought?).
demo.closing: The key proof is that assembling units into sentences that were never seen in training still works — the system does not memorize outputs, it builds them from reusable semantic pieces.
